lessons.title: The pre-snap read
lessons.objective: You can list what a quarterback checks before the snap.

payload.prompt: Before the snap, what does the quarterback scan most first?

options.text: Where the safeties line up and if they are one-high or two-high
The crowd noise level
The referee's position

explanation.correct: The safeties tell the quarterback what coverage is likely. One-high signals a single deep safety; two-high means two safeties split deep.
explanation.incorrect: The safety positions are the quarterback's first clue to coverage. That read shapes the entire play call.

payload.prompt: Tap where the quarterback looks first in his pre-snap read.

diagram.alt: A football field viewed from the offense showing the defense with two safeties at two-high depth.

explanation.correct: The safeties reveal the coverage shell. Read them first, then the linebackers, then the line.
explanation.incorrect: The quarterback's pre-snap read starts with safeties. Are they split (two-high) or stacked (one-high)? That changes everything.

payload.prompt: If a corner lines up 10 yards from the receiver before the snap, it is likely Cover 0 (man with no help). True or false?

scene.alt: A cornerback lined up tight on a receiver at the line of scrimmage, signaling press coverage or man coverage.

explanation.correct: True. A corner playing tight press coverage deep in the backfield is a tell for man coverage with no safety help.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a corner lined up so far off or so tight is a pre-snap clue that the defense is in man or Cover 0.

payload.prompt: Match each pre-snap tell to what it suggests.

pairs.definition: Likely Cover 2 or Cover 4; zone coverage is more likely than man.
Could be Cover 1, Cover 3, or Cover 0; man coverage is possible.
Blitz is coming; the quarterback might audible to hot routes or checkdowns.

explanation.summary: Pre-snap reads tell the quarterback where the help is (or is not). Safeties are the key.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-high: safe. One-high: risky. Blitz: hot route.

payload.prompt: You see a blitz coming. Do you audible to a screen pass or a go route?

facts.label: Defense
facts.value: Extra linebacker creeping up near the line

options.label: Audible to screen pass
options.consequence: Screen pass punishes aggressive blitz. The rusher has committed and the blockers are already set.
considerations: Screens are built to beat blitzes.
Go routes take time to develop and leave the QB exposed to the blitz.
A screen is a fast hit.

options.label: Try the go route anyway
options.consequence: A go route needs time. The extra rusher will get the quarterback before the receiver goes deep.
considerations: Deep routes take time to develop.
A blitz collapses time.

payload.expertNote: When you see a blitz pre-snap, audible to fast game: screens, checkdowns, and hitches. Do not run the slow play.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: He pointed at the Mike linebacker and nodded. That is when I knew the play was changing.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: The quarterback complimented the linebacker
The quarterback identified the blitz and made an audible
The center is changing the blocking scheme
The offense is signaling the defense

payload.translation: Pointing at the Mike (middle linebacker) is a pre-snap tell that the quarterback spotted something and called a new play to beat it.

followUps.line: Why would a quarterback point at the Mike?
followUps.why: Tells you the qb is actively reading the defense and making adjustments.

followUps.line: Does the defense change their play after the audible?
followUps.why: Tests if you know the Mike linebacker calls the coverage for the defense.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about what the quarterback is trying to communicate to his team at the line.

lessons.title: Route combinations
lessons.objective: You can describe flood, mesh and smash.

payload.prompt: In a flood concept, three receivers attack the same area to overload one defender. Tap where they are targeting.

diagram.alt: Three receivers running into a small zone area on one side of the field.

explanation.correct: Flood attacks one zone with three receivers, forcing the zone coverage to leave someone open.
explanation.incorrect: Flood is about numbers. Three on one zone creates an easy throw to whoever is open.

payload.prompt: In a mesh concept, two receivers cross over each other. What is the point?

options.text: To create confusion and rub off a man defender
To score a touchdown on the crossing
To line up side by side

explanation.correct: Mesh is a man-coverage killer. When receivers cross, they rub off defenders and create separation.
explanation.incorrect: The mesh is a crossing concept. Two receivers trade defenders by running over each other's paths.

payload.prompt: Match each route concept to what coverage it beats.

pairs.definition: Three receivers in one zone, beat zone coverage by overloading one defender with choices.
Two crossing routes, beat man coverage by rubbing off defenders.
Shallow slant and deep corner on the same side, beat Cover 3 by attacking the deep third.

explanation.summary: Concepts are answers to coverages. Know the coverage, find the combo that breaks it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Flood beats zone. Mesh beats man. Smash attacks the third.

payload.prompt: A flood concept is designed to overload zone coverage by putting three receivers in a small area. True or false?

scene.alt: Three receivers converging into one zone area with two defenders in coverage.

explanation.correct: True. Flood is a zone-killing concept. Zone defenders cover areas, so three receivers in one zone creates a mismatch.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, flood is for zone coverage. Too many receivers in one zone creates an open one.

payload.prompt: You see Cover 3 (three deep thirds, four underneath in zone). Do you call mesh or smash?

options.label: Call smash concept
options.consequence: Smash has a deep corner into the one-third you are attacking. Beat the deep third and the underneath zone opens.
considerations: Smash attacks the deep third with one receiver and the other at intermediate depth.
If the deep third bites on the corner, the intermediate is open.
Mesh is better against man coverage.

options.label: Call mesh concept
options.consequence: Mesh is for man coverage. Against Cover 3 zone, the crossing receivers just switch zone defenders, no advantage.
considerations: Mesh is a man-coverage concept.
Zone coverage is not troubled by crosses.
Use zone-beaters like flood or smash instead.

payload.expertNote: Know your coverage. Mesh beats man (rubbing off defenders). Smash and flood beat zone (overload or attack the third).

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That is a classic mesh out of 11 personnel. Two receivers crossing, one outside, one in the slot. Man coverage is finished.

payload.question: What is about to happen?

options.text: The running back will block
One receiver will be open because the defenders rubbed off each other
The quarterback will take a sack
The defense will blitz

payload.translation: A mesh concept against man coverage is nearly impossible to defend. Two receivers crossing create unavoidable picks and rubs on man defenders.

followUps.line: Why does mesh work against man and not zone?
followUps.why: Tests your understanding of the difference: man is one-on-one; zone covers areas. Mesh rubs off one-on-one matchups.
Shows you know the code: 1 back, 1 tight end, 3 receivers.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about what happens when two receivers cross paths and there is a defender on each one.

lessons.title: Reading progression
lessons.objective: You can explain a quarterback's first, second and third read.

payload.prompt: Arrange these in the order a quarterback checks receivers.

items.text: Second read: secondary receiver, deeper or across
Third read: tertiary receiver, usually on a route behind the sticks
Checkdown: running back on a short route to the flat if everyone else is covered

explanation.correct: The quarterback works through the progression from first to checkdown. If the first is covered, he looks to the second.
explanation.incorrect: Progressions are in order: primary first, secondary second, tertiary third, checkdown last.

payload.prompt: The first read in a progression is usually?

options.text: The running back in the flat
The primary receiver, the one the play is designed for
Whichever receiver is running the deepest

explanation.correct: The play is designed around one receiver, usually deep or intermediate. That is the first read.
explanation.incorrect: The first read is the receiver the play is built for. The second and third are alternatives if he is covered.

payload.prompt: A quarterback who gets to the checkdown quickly is making a good decision. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback scanning receivers downfield, then quickly finding a running back in the flat.

explanation.correct: True. Going through a progression and getting to the checkdown fast is smart. Better a safe five yards than a sack.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, if the first and second reads are covered, the checkdown is the right choice. Fast decisions beat pressure.

payload.prompt: Why do quarterbacks have a progression if they could just throw it to whoever is open?

options.text: The play is called with a specific receiver in mind; the progression is built around that read
The quarterback is not good at finding open receivers
It confuses the defense before the snap

explanation.correct: Every play is designed with a primary read. The progression is the plan for if that read is covered.
explanation.incorrect: Progressions are pre-planned. The quarterback knows the order he is checking receivers because the play dictates it.

payload.prompt: First and second reads covered, checkdown open for five yards. Go or wait for third?

facts.label: Checkdown
facts.value: Open, running back in the flat

options.label: Throw the checkdown
options.consequence: Five yards beats a sack. If pressure is arriving, the checkdown is the right call.
considerations: The pocket is collapsing.
Five yards is better than negative yards.
Live to play the next down.

options.label: Wait for the third read
options.consequence: Pressure arrives before the third read develops. The quarterback takes a sack.
considerations: The progression takes time.
Pressure is in the pocket now.

payload.expertNote: Progressions are fast-paced. If the first and second are covered and pressure is coming, take the checkdown. Game management beats heroics.

payload.prompt: Match each position in the progression to what it represents.

pairs.definition: The primary receiver, the one the play is built for.
The alternative receiver if the first is covered.
The running back or slot receiver for a quick, safe throw to avoid a sack.

explanation.summary: Progressions move from primary to alternative to checkdown: all by design.
explanation.sayThisLine: First is the plan. Second is the backup. Checkdown is survival.

lessons.title: Pressure count
lessons.objective: You can find the free rusher and choose the right answer.

payload.prompt: In a protection scheme, blocking assignments are made based on?

options.text: Reading the rushers and assigning each blocker to stop one
The quarterback's favorite target
The team with the loudest crowd

explanation.correct: The center usually calls the protection scheme, assigning players to block the most dangerous rushers.
explanation.incorrect: Protection is about numbers: blockers versus rushers. Identify the threat, assign a blocker to each one.

payload.prompt: If the offense has five blockers and the defense sends five rushers, one rusher is always free. True or false?

scene.alt: Five offensive blockers lined up against five defensive rushers.

explanation.correct: True. In a numbers game, five blockers stop four rushers and one gets free. The protection must account for this with a hot route.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, math matters. Blockers versus rushers determines if someone is open.

payload.prompt: Match each protection concept to what it addresses.

pairs.definition: The offensive line and running back block the front four rushers.
An extra blocker (often running back or tight end) stays to block a blitzing linebacker or safety.
A receiver changes his route to become a checkdown and pickup a free rusher, turning him into a passer.

explanation.summary: Protection is about matching numbers. Hot routes solve the free-rusher problem.
explanation.sayThisLine: Count rushers. Assign blockers. Hot route is the insurance.

payload.prompt: You see a blitz coming: six rushers, five blockers. Do you audible to a hot route or trust the protection?

options.label: Audible to a hot route
options.consequence: A hot route turns the free rusher into a target. The receiver picks him up and becomes an outlet.
considerations: You have six rushers on five blockers.
Someone is free.
Hot route solves this math problem.

options.label: Trust the protection
options.consequence: One rusher gets free and crushes the quarterback. No time for the deep play to develop.
considerations: Math does not work.
One free rusher ends the play fast.

payload.expertNote: Blitz math: if there are more rushers than blockers, audible to a hot route. Turn the free rusher into a target.

statement.speaker: Center
statement.text: Mike! Mike! Two! Two! The linebacker is your guy, running back picks him up!

payload.question: What is the center doing?

options.text: Calling out his favorite plays
Identifying the middle linebacker and assigning a blitz pick-up
Telling the quarterback to throw
Disagreeing with the defensive call

payload.translation: The center is identifying the Mike (middle linebacker) and telling the running back he is the assignment for pick-up to stop the blitz.

followUps.line: Who usually calls out the protection?
followUps.why: Tests your knowledge that the center is the quarterback of the defense... wait, the offense. The center calls the line protection.

followUps.line: Why point out the Mike specifically?
followUps.why: The middle linebacker is the most likely to blitz from the linebacker level.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about who is directing the blockers at the line on offense.

lessons.title: Run gaps
lessons.objective: You can name the gap a run hits and who is responsible for it.

payload.prompt: Tap the A gap (the space between the center and guard on the offense's left).

diagram.alt: An offensive line showing the gaps between each lineman.

explanation.correct: A gap is between the center and guard. B gap is between guard and tackle. C gap is outside the tackle.
explanation.incorrect: Gaps are the spaces between linemen. A, B, C from inside to outside.

payload.prompt: In inside zone, the running back reads the blockers and takes the first crease. Which gap is he likely using?

options.text: The A or B gap, straight up the middle
Always the C gap outside
Whichever gap the left guard opens

explanation.correct: Inside zone is between the tackles. The back reads the blocks and cuts through the A or B gap depending on where the seam opens.
explanation.incorrect: Inside zone runs close to the middle, typically through the A or B gap.

payload.prompt: Outside zone is designed to stretch the play sideways and attack the C gap. True or false?

scene.alt: A running back stretching the play horizontally along the edge, looking to plant and cut upfield.

explanation.correct: True. Outside zone stretches it sideways, then the back plants and cuts up through the C gap or further out.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, outside zone goes wide first, then the back cuts upfield. C gap and edge are the targets.

payload.prompt: Match each gap assignment to who is responsible.

pairs.definition: Linebacker or safety assigned to the space between center and guard.
Linebacker or edge rusher filling the space between guard and tackle.
Edge rusher (DE or OLB) responsible for the space outside the tackle.

explanation.summary: Defense assigns gap responsibilities so every run lane is covered. Gap scheme tells each defender his job.
explanation.sayThisLine: A gap: center-guard. B gap: guard-tackle. C gap: outside tackle.

payload.prompt: The running back bursts into the B gap and sees it is stuffed. Cut left (A gap) or bounce it outside (C gap)?

options.label: Cut back to the A gap
options.consequence: The blocker has a seal in the A gap. Cutback gains three to five yards against the grain.
considerations: The blocker is winning his block in the A gap.
The B gap is lost.
Cutback is the backup plan.

options.label: Bounce it to the edge
options.consequence: The edge rusher is reaching and has good leverage. Bouncing it outside loses yards.
considerations: The C gap edge is not sealed.
He will make the tackle.

payload.expertNote: Inside zone reads: if the primary gap (B) is stuffed, cutback to the secondary (A). Outside zone: if the edge is free, cut back.

lessons.title: Throwing windows
lessons.objective: You can see why the same throw works on one snap and fails on the next.

payload.prompt: The throwing window for a receiver is narrowest when?

options.text: The receiver is running away from the quarterback
A defender is approaching the receiver from the side or back
The receiver is young and inexperienced

explanation.correct: When a defender closes on the receiver, the window shrinks fast. The quarterback must throw before the defender can bat it.
explanation.incorrect: The window is the space between defenders. A defender closing makes it smaller or shuts it down completely.

payload.prompt: Anticipation throw: QB throws before receiver breaks, to where he will be. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback throwing the ball with anticipation before a receiver makes his break.

explanation.correct: True. Anticipation throws beat tight windows and quick-closing defenders. The ball arrives before the receiver even breaks.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, anticipation is about timing, not waiting. Throw to where he will be, not where he is.

payload.prompt: Match each throw type to what the window depends on.

pairs.definition: Long window; the receiver is far from defenders. Biggest vertical separation.
Defenders are close; throw must be precise and fast to beat coverage.
The receiver's ability to run after catching the ball. A good receiver turns three yards into ten.

explanation.summary: Windows open and close based on defender proximity. Great receivers turn short throws into big plays (YAC).
explanation.sayThisLine: Deep = wide window. Tight = fast throw. YAC = receiver skill.

payload.prompt: A defender is playing inside coverage on your receiver. Back-shoulder throw or front-shoulder?

facts.label: Defender
facts.value: Playing inside shade (closer to his inside)

facts.label: Window
facts.value: Only the back shoulder is open

options.label: Back-shoulder throw
options.consequence: Only the receiver can reach the back shoulder. The defender cannot get there, and the receiver shields the ball.
considerations: The defender is in position to cut inside.
Back shoulder is the only window.
The receiver uses his body to protect the ball.

options.label: Front-shoulder throw
options.consequence: The defender is already playing inside. Front shoulder is the defender's area, and he will likely intercept.
considerations: The defender is between the quarterback and the front shoulder.
Easy pick.

payload.expertNote: Back-shoulder throws exploit tight coverage. Throw to the shoulder the defender cannot reach. The receiver shields the ball.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That window closed in a heartbeat. The corner blinked and the safety helped. One more step and the quarterback is sacked.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: The receiver was not open
The throwing window collapsed because defenders were closing fast
The quarterback threw the ball late
The defense was celebrating too early

payload.translation: A tight throwing window exists only for a moment. As defenders close, the space shrinks. The quarterback must throw fast or the window closes entirely.

followUps.line: How does a quarterback keep windows open?
followUps.why: Tests your knowledge: quick release, anticipation, receiver separation.

followUps.line: Can a window close so fast the quarterback never gets to throw?
followUps.why: Yes—if pressure arrives too fast or the receiver is not open.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about how much space a ball can fit through between two defenders.

lessons.title: Zone or gap
lessons.objective: You can tell zone blocking from a gap scheme.

payload.prompt: In zone blocking, each lineman blocks an area and the running back reads the blockers to pick his hole. True or false?

scene.alt: An offensive line moving together, blocking an area rather than specific defenders.

explanation.correct: True. Zone blocking is about movement and reading. The back finds the seam created by the blocking combination.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, zone blocking is collaborative. The line moves together, and the back picks the open gap.

payload.prompt: Match each blocking scheme to how it works.

pairs.definition: Linemen block an area together, and the back reads the blocks to find the open crease.
Each lineman has one defender to block, often with a puller leading the way.
A pulling guard leads the way, wiping out a linebacker for the back to follow.

explanation.summary: Zone: read and adjust. Gap: execute your job.
explanation.sayThisLine: Zone is flow. Gap is assignment.

payload.prompt: A pulling guard in a gap-scheme run is designed to?

options.text: Lead block for the running back by wiping out a linebacker
Pull back to protect the quarterback
Go downfield to block a receiver

explanation.correct: A puller leads the way, blocking a linebacker and opening a hole for the running back to follow.
explanation.incorrect: The pulling guard is a lead blocker on gap runs like power. He clears a path.

payload.prompt: Your defense is loaded up on the edge. Zone block or gap block to attack inside?

facts.label: Inside
facts.value: Light box (fewer defenders in the middle)

facts.label: Desired result
facts.value: Get the ball into the open middle

options.label: Zone block
options.consequence: Zone gives the back the flexibility to cut back or bounce out. With a light box, he finds grass inside.
considerations: Zone is adaptable.
The back can read and find the open gap.
Light box means inside is open.

options.label: Gap block
options.consequence: Gap scheme with inside assignments works, but it is more rigid. If the back needs to adjust, he is limited.
considerations: Gap is assignment-based.
Less flexibility for the back to read.

payload.expertNote: Zone blocks are more adaptable. Gap blocks are reliable but need the right read. Against a light box, zone gives the back more options.

payload.prompt: The main difference between zone and gap blocking is?

options.text: Zone is for passes; gap is for runs
Zone is movement and reading; gap is assignment and execution
They are the same, just with different names

explanation.correct: Zone blocking emphasizes reading and adapting. Gap blocking is about each blocker doing his job on one defender.
explanation.incorrect: The philosophies are opposite. Zone: flexible and reactive. Gap: rigid and predictable.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: Watch the left guard. He is pulling across the formation to lead the back on the power run.

payload.question: What blocking scheme is this?

options.text: Zone blocking
Gap blocking, with a pull to the second level
Play-action blocking
Pass protection

payload.translation: A pulling guard is a signature of gap-scheme runs like power, counter and toss. He clears the path for the running back.

followUps.line: Why do pulling guards only show up in gap schemes?
followUps.why: In gap, each blocker has a job; a pull is that job. In zone, everyone stays put and blocks an area.
Usually a linebacker who would be in the gap or second level.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about what a player pulling means: he is stepping back and moving to another spot, not staying in place.

lessons.title: Short yardage
lessons.objective: You can explain the sneak and why teams love it.

payload.prompt: Third and one. Sneak or hand it off?

facts.label: Defense
facts.value: Spread and light on the line

options.label: Quarterback sneak
options.consequence: The QB sneaks behind a surge, gets one yard easily, and keeps the offense on schedule.
considerations: One yard is all you need.
The sneak is nearly automatic from one yard.
No handoff to a back, less chance of a fumble.

options.label: Hand off to the running back
options.consequence: The back powers through for one yard, but the sneak is safer.
considerations: Still gets one yard.
More moving parts means more chance of error.

payload.expertNote: On short yardage, the sneak is nearly automatic. One yard is nothing for a quarterback pushing behind a surging line.

payload.prompt: Why is the quarterback sneak so hard to stop?

options.text: The offense moves the entire line forward in a surge, and the QB follows the big mass
The quarterback is faster than defensive linemen
The defense is not allowed to touch the quarterback on a sneak

explanation.correct: The sneak works because the whole line surges forward together. The defense has no time to stack the box.
explanation.incorrect: The sneak is about synchronized power from the line, not the quarterback's individual speed.

payload.prompt: Tush push: QB sneak with teammates pushing from behind. Legal in 2026. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback being pushed forward by teammates on a short-yardage play, gaining yards with assistance.

explanation.correct: True. The tush push is a sneak where teammates give the QB a shove from behind. Legal in the NFL as of 2026.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the tush push is a short-yardage power play where teammates assist the QB forward. It remains legal.

payload.prompt: Match each short-yardage call to when to use it.

pairs.definition: Third or fourth and one or two; automatic when you need a yard or less.
Third and one or two; a pulling guard leads the running back.
Goal line; the running back dives straight ahead with the line surging.

explanation.summary: Short yardage: sneak for the QB, power for the back, dive near the goal line.
explanation.sayThisLine: One yard? Sneak. Heavy? Power. Goal line? Dive.

payload.prompt: The tush push debate is about?

options.text: Whether teammates pushing the quarterback is fair or unfair
Whether the quarterback should get more playing time
Whether short yardage plays should exist

explanation.correct: Some fans say the sneak with a push is unstoppable and unfair. Others say it is legal, creative football.
explanation.incorrect: The tush push is controversial because it seems almost impossible to defend when legal.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Fourth and one. Give me the sneak. We get it, we live. We miss, we did not have it anyway.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: The team should always go for it on fourth and one
On fourth and one, the sneak is nearly automatic and worth the risk
The quarterback is the best player on the team
The offense is out of ideas

payload.translation: Fourth-and-one decisions favor going for it now, and the sneak is the highest-percentage play in short yardage.

followUps.line: Why does modern coaching favor going for it on fourth and one?
followUps.why: Tests EPA understanding: analytics say it improves win probability.

followUps.line: Would the coach sneak on fourth and five?
followUps.why: No; five yards is too far, even for a sneak.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about the simplicity: QB follows the line forward one yard on fourth and one.
